picks.style: greek tragic lament, solo aulos and sparse lyre, keening female voice, very slow, bare, desolate
picks.why: Electra over the urn — 'accept me into this abode of yours, me, a nothing, into your nothingness.'

picks.style: ancient chorus with soloist, lyre and frame drum, layered voices answering one voice, solemn, circling, building
picks.why: The kommos on grief that will not end: the bird crying Itys, Itys, and Niobe weeping in her rock.

picks.style: solemn georgian nocturne, chamber organ and low strings, grave baritone, slow, hushed, funereal
picks.why: 'Tired Nature's sweet restorer, balmy Sleep!' — the most famous opening in the graveyard school, and it holds alone.

picks.style: english blank-verse meditation, viola da gamba and single bell, low male voice, measured, austere, tolling
picks.why: 'Our birth is nothing but our death begun; / As tapers waste that instant they take fire.'

picks.style: georgian moral ode, harpsichord and strings, declamatory tenor, steady, ironic, gathering
picks.why: 'That all men are about to live' — forever on the brink of being born, the whole poem's argument in one line.

picks.style: georgian comic ballad, fiddle and harpsichord, wry baritone patter, brisk, jaunty, gallows-humoured
picks.why: The condemned man and the priest, ending on a real punchline: 'He that's hang'd before Noon, ought to think of To-night.'

picks.style: drawing-room satirical song, plucked harpsichord and light strings, arch mezzo, light, clipped, knowing
picks.why: Marriage anatomised in couplets — 'He sighs for Freedom, She for Pow'r.'

picks.style: classical hymn art song, baroque strings and harp, clear tenor, stately, bright, ceremonial
picks.why: Infant Zeus in a golden cradle, the bee distilling honey on his lips while the Curetes clash their arms to drown his crying.

picks.style: scottish parlour ballad, fiddle and small harp, plaintive female voice, slow, lilting, refrain-led
picks.why: Built on a returning line — 'Dim is the Star of Eden vale' — closing on 'The Sun is set in Eden vale.'

picks.style: scots ballad lament, harp and low strings, clear female voice, unhurried, grey, sea-swept
picks.why: A lady in white weeping on the shore while the lightning walks the waste and she does not flinch.

picks.style: georgian comic air, harpsichord and pizzicato strings, arch female voice, quick, teasing, light
picks.why: A whole joke with its own refrain — 'O! it were well for woman kind / Were all their loss a tooth!'

picks.style: archaic greek hymn, kithara and low drone, deep male voice, slow, oracular, weighty
picks.why: The Hesiodic hymn to Zeus — lightly he gives strength, lightly he crushes the strong — with its own hammering repetition.

picks.style: greek epitaph chant, single lyre, distant clear voice, still, timeless, sparse
picks.why: The bronze maiden on Midas' tomb: so long as water flows and tall trees flourish, she will keep saying it.

picks.style: chivalric epic recitation, viol and lute, warm baritone, measured, noble, unhurried
picks.why: Two enemies trading armour instead of blows, so that others may see they were hosts and guests in their fathers' time.

picks.style: classical greek gnomic song, lyre and soft drone, grave male voice, slow, reflective, plain
picks.why: Not gold nor diamond nor loaded fields, but 'gallant men's unanimous resolve' — a complete argument in verse.

picks.style: victorian nursery rhyme, music box and pizzicato strings, bright playful voice, quick, light, sing-song
picks.why: The only candidate, and it happens to be a finished song already — Jack Sprat, whole and singable.
